In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
macroprolactins are not detected by the low-reading methods, but are detected by medium- and high-reading immunoassays (6)(7).

macroprolactins have been shown to be present in the circulation of a significant number of patients with hyperprolactinaemia, but the prevalence of this condition in the general population has not been determined (5).
macroprolactinaemia is a common phenomenon that can lead to false positive results with immunoassays, which can be identified by using the Prolactin Macro Assay (PMA) kit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the measurement of macroprolaktin in serum samples is not straightforward and requires the use of different methods.
the Prolac 2 assay is a low-reader, the Immulite PRL assay is a medium-reader, and the Nichols Advantage assay is a high-reader.
the measurement of macroprolaltin is method and sample dependent, and it is not possible to predict which method would detect macroprolactins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of macroprolctin in a patient sample should be considered when the PRL concentration in that sample is higher than 1000 ng/mL.
the presence of macroprolectin in patient samples can lead to false-positive results for PRL, depending on the assay method and the sample matrix.

macroprolactinaemia should not be diagnosed by immunoassay alone, and the presence of macroprolactalinaemia should always be confirmed by gel filtration chromatography (GCF) and/or polyethylene glycol precipitation.
